1.4.1:
Why this matters

Six Sigma makes processes consistent. Lean makes them fast and free of waste. Many problems in real operations, from long lead times to piles of work waiting, are Lean problems, not variation problems. Knowing Lean's principles and vocabulary lets you recognize which kind of problem you face.

The big idea

Lean starts from one question: what does the customer actually value? Everything else in the process is either necessary support or waste. Lean removes the waste so that value flows to the customer quickly, smoothly, and only when it is needed.

Most processes are shockingly slow when you look closely. A shipment might take 30 hours from order to delivery, but only about 3 hours of that is something the customer values: picking, loading, driving, unloading. The rest is waiting.

Only the dark slivers are value-added. Lean attacks the light part.

The five Lean principles

James Womack and Daniel Jones summarized Lean in five principles (Lean Thinking, 1996):

  1. Specify value: define value from the customer's point of view: what they want, when, at what price. Not what is convenient for us to make.
  2. Map the value stream: identify every step, for one product or service, from request to delivery. Mark which steps create value and which do not.
  3. Create flow: make the value-creating steps happen one after another without stopping, waiting or batching.
  4. Establish pull: produce only when the customer (or the next step) asks for it, instead of pushing work through on a forecast.
  5. Pursue perfection: repeat the cycle forever. Each round exposes more waste.

Value-added and non-value-added

Recall from 1.2.1:

  • Value-added (VA): the customer would pay for it; it changes the product or service toward what they want; done right the first time.
  • Necessary non-value-added (NNVA): the customer would not pay for it, but it is required for now (regulation, safety, accounting).
  • Non-value-added (NVA): pure waste. Remove it.

Push vs pull, flow vs batch

Push builds piles between steps; pull keeps work moving only as fast as it is used.

  • Push: each step works to a schedule or forecast and sends its output on, whether or not the next step is ready. Result: inventory piles up, lead time grows, and problems hide in the piles.
  • Pull: a step produces only when the next step (ultimately the customer) signals it has used something. A kanban (signal card, empty bin, electronic signal) carries that signal upstream.
  • Batch processing: do a big batch at one step, then move the whole batch to the next. Every item waits for its whole batch at every step.
  • One-piece flow (single-piece or continuous flow): each item moves to the next step as soon as it is done. Lead time drops dramatically, and a defect is noticed after one piece instead of after a whole batch.

Muda, mura and muri

Toyota describes three enemies of a smooth process:

  • Muda (waste): activity that adds no value. The seven (or eight) wastes in 1.4.4.
  • Mura (unevenness): irregular workload, such as 40 trailers arriving Monday and 5 on Friday. Unevenness causes waste because capacity must be sized for the peak.
  • Muri (overburden): pushing people or equipment beyond what they can sustain. It causes breakdowns, injuries and mistakes.

Leveling the work (removing mura) prevents overburden (muri), which in turn reduces waste (muda).

Lean vocabulary

Learn one line for each:

  • Takt time: available time ÷ customer demand; the beat the process must keep (see 1.2.5).
  • Kaizen: continuous, incremental improvement, often in short focused events ("kaizen events" or "kaizen blitzes").
  • Gemba: "the real place", where the work happens. Going to see it is a "gemba walk".
  • SMED (single-minute exchange of die): methods to make changeovers very fast, which makes small batches affordable.
  • TPM (total productive maintenance): operators take part in routine care of their equipment to prevent breakdowns.
  • Jidoka: automation with a human touch; machines or processes stop automatically when a problem occurs, so defects are never passed on.
  • Heijunka: leveling production by volume and mix over time.
  • Andon: a visual signal (light, board, cord) showing status and calling for help when there is a problem.
  • Standard work: the current best, documented way to do a task, including sequence, timing and inventory. It is the baseline for improvement.
  • Poka-yoke: mistake-proofing (5.1).
  • Kanban: a signal that authorizes production or movement in a pull system.

The two pillars

Toyota's approach rests on continuous improvement (always finding and removing waste) and respect for people (the people doing the work are the experts, and improvement is done with them, not to them). Tools without respect for people do not last.

Worked example

A trailer repair shop takes 9 days on average to return a trailer, but total hands-on repair time is 6 hours.

  1. Value-added time: 6 hours. Lead time: 9 days = 216 hours. Process cycle efficiency = 6 ÷ 216 ≈ 2.8%.
  2. Value stream walk: trailers wait for inspection (1 day), wait for a parts order (4 days), wait in queue for a bay (3 days).
  3. Lean responses: inspect on arrival (flow), stock the most common parts with a kanban (pull), level the arrival schedule with the fleet team (heijunka).

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Value is defined by the customer, not by the company or the engineer.
  • Lean is not just cost cutting. It is about flow and lead time; cost falls as a result.
  • Pull is not "make to order only". It means producing in response to actual use, often with small buffers controlled by kanban.
  • Kaizen means incremental improvement, not a one-time big project.

Check yourself

  1. List the five Lean principles in order.
  2. What is the difference between push and pull?
  3. Which of muda, mura and muri describes a workload of 40 trailers Monday and 5 Friday?
  4. What is jidoka?
  5. Lead time is 20 days; value-added time is 4 hours. What is the process cycle efficiency?
Show answers
  1. Specify value, map the value stream, create flow, establish pull, pursue perfection.
  2. Push produces to a schedule regardless of need; pull produces only when the next step signals it has used something.
  3. Mura (unevenness).
  4. Stopping automatically when a problem occurs so defects are not passed on ("automation with a human touch").
  5. 4 ÷ (20 × 24) = 4 ÷ 480 ≈ 0.8%.

Key takeaways

  • Five principles: value, value stream, flow, pull, perfection.
  • Value is defined by the customer; most lead time is waiting.
  • Pull and one-piece flow beat push and batches for lead time and quality.
  • Muda (waste), mura (unevenness), muri (overburden).
  • Pillars: continuous improvement and respect for people.
1.4.2:
Why this matters

Like 1.1.2, this is a matching topic: who developed which idea. The story is short and memorable because it follows one company, Toyota, with a few key people.

The story

Before Toyota: Henry Ford (1910s). Ford's moving assembly line (1913) made the Model T in a continuous flow, slashing the time and cost to build a car. Ford is a precursor to Lean: he understood flow. But his system relied on huge volumes of one product ("any color so long as it is black") and big inventories.

Sakichi Toyoda (around 1900 to the 1920s). Founder of the Toyoda family business, Sakichi invented power looms that stopped automatically when a thread broke. One worker could tend many machines, and no defective cloth was made. This is the origin of jidoka: building quality in by stopping at the first sign of a problem.

Kiichiro Toyoda (1930s). Sakichi's son started Toyota's car business and promoted the idea of just-in-time: making only what is needed, when it is needed, in the amount needed.

Taiichi Ohno (late 1940s to 1970s). Toyota's production engineer and executive who built the Toyota Production System (TPS). Post-war Japan had little money, little space, and a market that wanted many models in small quantities, so mass production would not work. Ohno developed just-in-time and pull production, kanban, and the idea of the seven wastes. He was inspired partly by American supermarkets, where shelves are restocked only when customers take items.

Shigeo Shingo (1950s to 1970s). An industrial engineer and consultant who worked with Toyota. He developed SMED (quick changeover) and poka-yoke (mistake-proofing), and wrote some of the first books explaining TPS to the West.

How "Lean" got its name

In the late 1980s, MIT's International Motor Vehicle Program studied car makers worldwide. Researcher John Krafcik coined the term "lean" (1988) for Toyota's approach, because it used less of everything: less space, inventory, effort and time. James Womack, Daniel Jones and Daniel Roos published the program's findings in The Machine That Changed the World (1990), which made Lean famous. Womack and Jones then wrote Lean Thinking (1996), which set out the five principles.

Timeline

WhenWhoWhat
1913Henry FordMoving assembly line (flow)
~1900 to 1920sSakichi ToyodaSelf-stopping loom (jidoka)
1930sKiichiro ToyodaJust-in-time idea at Toyota
1940s to 1970sTaiichi OhnoToyota Production System, kanban, pull, seven wastes
1950s to 1970sShigeo ShingoSMED, poka-yoke
1988John KrafcikCoined "lean"
1990Womack, Jones, RoosThe Machine That Changed the World
1996Womack, JonesLean Thinking, five principles

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Ohno vs Shingo. Ohno: TPS, kanban, just-in-time, seven wastes. Shingo: SMED and poka-yoke.
  • Toyoda vs Toyota. The family name is Toyoda; the company became Toyota.
  • Ford was a precursor, not the inventor of Lean. He had flow, but not pull or flexibility.
  • Krafcik named it; Womack and Jones popularized it.

Check yourself

  1. Who developed SMED?
  2. What did Sakichi Toyoda's loom contribute to Lean?
  3. Which book introduced "lean production" to a wide audience, and when?
  4. What inspired Ohno's pull system?
  5. Put in order: Lean Thinking, Ford's moving line, Krafcik coins "lean", TPS developed.
Show answers
  1. Shigeo Shingo.
  2. Jidoka: stopping automatically when a problem occurs.
  3. The Machine That Changed the World (1990), by Womack, Jones and Roos.
  4. American supermarkets, which restock shelves as customers take items.
  5. Ford's moving line (1913), TPS developed (1940s to 70s), Krafcik coins "lean" (1988), Lean Thinking (1996).

Key takeaways

  • Ford: flow. Sakichi Toyoda: jidoka. Kiichiro Toyoda: just-in-time idea.
  • Ohno: TPS, pull, kanban, seven wastes. Shingo: SMED, poka-yoke.
  • Krafcik coined "lean"; Womack and Jones popularized it (1990, 1996).
1.4.3:
Why this matters

Organizations today mostly use the combination, Lean Six Sigma. Knowing what each half is good at tells you which tools to pick for a given problem, and exam scenarios often ask exactly that.

The big idea

They attack different enemies:

LeanSix Sigma
EnemyWasteVariation
Main goalSpeed, flow, short lead timeConsistency, few defects
Key question"Why does this take so long?""Why is this so inconsistent?"
Typical toolsValue stream map, 5S, kanban, SMED, standard workStatistics, MSA, hypothesis tests, regression, SPC
Typical resultsShorter lead time, less inventory, less spaceFewer defects, higher capability, lower COPQ

Both are customer-focused and data-driven, and they need each other. A fast process that makes defects just makes defects faster. A consistent process full of waiting is reliably slow.

Why they fit together

  • Waste hides variation: piles of inventory mask defects and erratic steps. Lean removes the piles so variation becomes visible.
  • Variation creates waste: inconsistent output forces safety stock, rework and inspection. Six Sigma reduces variation so Lean flow can work.
  • Lean tools fit inside DMAIC:
  • Define: SIPOC, VOC.
  • Measure: value stream map, takt time, process cycle efficiency.
  • Analyze: the seven wastes, constraint analysis.
  • Improve: 5S, SMED, kanban, flow cells, mistake-proofing.
  • Control: standard work, visual management.

Which to use

  • Symptoms like "slow", "waiting", "long lead time", "too much inventory", "piles of work", "handoffs" point to Lean.
  • Symptoms like "inconsistent", "variable", "defects", "out of specification", "rework rate", "customer complaints about errors" point to Six Sigma.
  • Many real problems have both. Lean Six Sigma uses both tool sets inside one DMAIC project.

If the solution is already known and simple, neither a DMAIC project nor a big Lean event is needed: just do it.

Worked example

Classify the main approach for each:

  1. "Claims take 42 days to resolve; each spends most of that in someone's inbox." Lean: waiting and flow.
  2. "Trailer weights at the scale vary widely, and 6% are overweight." Six Sigma: variation against a specification.
  3. "Invoices take 10 days and 8% have errors." Both: Lean for the 10 days, Six Sigma for the 8%.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Lean = waste/speed; Six Sigma = variation/defects. Look for those words in scenarios.
  • They are complementary, not competing.
  • Lean tools are used inside DMAIC, not in a separate method.

Check yourself

  1. What is the main enemy of Lean? Of Six Sigma?
  2. A process has huge queues between steps but very few defects. Which approach first?
  3. Name a Lean tool used in the Improve phase.
  4. Why does waste hide variation?
  5. What do Lean and Six Sigma have in common?
Show answers
  1. Lean: waste. Six Sigma: variation.
  2. Lean, because the problem is flow and waiting.
  3. Any of: 5S, SMED, kanban, one-piece flow, mistake-proofing, standard work.
  4. Inventory and queues absorb and hide erratic performance and defects, so problems are not seen.
  5. Both are customer-focused, data-driven and aimed at continuous improvement.

Key takeaways

  • Lean: waste, flow, speed. Six Sigma: variation, defects, consistency.
  • Complementary: waste hides variation; variation creates waste.
  • Lean tools sit inside DMAIC phases.
  • Scenario words: delay and waiting point to Lean; inconsistency and defects point to Six Sigma.
1.4.4:
Why this matters

You cannot remove waste you cannot see. The seven wastes give you a checklist for "learning to see". Classification questions, "which waste is this?", are very common on the exam.

The big idea

Taiichi Ohno identified seven categories of waste (muda): activities that use time, effort or money but add nothing the customer values. IASSC names them:

  1. Overproduction
  2. Correction
  3. Inventory
  4. Motion
  5. Overprocessing
  6. Conveyance
  7. Waiting

Many other materials use different names for two of them, with the memory aid TIMWOOD: Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Waiting, Overproduction, Overprocessing, Defects. The cross-walk:

  • Correction = Defects
  • Conveyance = Transportation

Each waste explained

Overproduction: making more, or sooner, than the customer needs.
Printing and staging all of tomorrow's paperwork today; loading trailers "just in case" before orders confirm; producing to forecast. It is often called the worst waste because it causes the others: extra product must be stored (inventory), moved (conveyance), handled (motion), and may become damaged or obsolete (correction).

Correction (defects): fixing mistakes.
Rework, re-delivery, correcting invoices, re-doing paperwork, handling claims. Everything spent finding and fixing errors.

Inventory: more material or work than is needed right now.
Excess spare parts, full yards of trailers waiting, stacks of unprocessed claims, emails waiting in an inbox. Inventory ties up money and space, and hides problems.

Motion: unnecessary movement of people.
Walking to the other end of the dock for a pallet jack, searching for tools, reaching, bending, clicking through ten screens. The person moves, not the product.

Overprocessing: doing more than the customer needs.
Double data entry, extra approvals, reports nobody reads, polishing a part beyond its specification, three signatures where one would do.

Conveyance (transportation): unnecessary movement of materials or information.
Moving freight between docks twice, routing documents through extra departments, sending a trailer to a yard and back. The product moves, but nothing about it improves. (For a carrier, moving freight to the customer is the value-added service; moving it around the terminal unnecessarily is the waste.)

Waiting: people or things idle, waiting for the next step.
Drivers waiting at the dock, trucks waiting for paperwork, an order waiting for credit approval, a technician waiting for parts.

The eighth waste

Many organizations add an eighth: unused talent (or skills, or human potential). Not using people's knowledge, ideas and abilities, for example never asking drivers how to improve routing. The memory aid becomes DOWNTIME: Defects, Overproduction, Waiting, Non-utilized talent, Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Extra processing.

Telling similar wastes apart

  • Motion vs conveyance: motion = people moving; conveyance = materials or information moving.
  • Overprocessing vs correction: overprocessing = doing more than needed (on a good product); correction = fixing what was done wrong.
  • Overproduction vs inventory: overproduction is the act of making too much too soon; inventory is the resulting stock (it can also come from other causes, such as big purchase lots).
  • Waiting: the thing or person is idle; nothing is happening to it.

Worked example

Classify each at a distribution center:

ObservationWaste
300 pallets of last season's product in racksInventory
Picker walks 200 m to the printer for each pick listMotion
Orders keyed into the warehouse system and again into a spreadsheetOverprocessing
Pallets moved from receiving to a holding area, then to the racksConveyance
Shipping waits 40 minutes for the trailer to be releasedWaiting
Wrong item shipped, return and re-shipCorrection
Picking tomorrow's orders today "to get ahead"Overproduction

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Double data entry is overprocessing, not correction (nothing was wrong).
  • Walking to get tools is motion, not conveyance.
  • Excess WIP is inventory.
  • Overproduction drives the other wastes; it is called the worst.
  • IASSC wording: remember Correction = Defects and Conveyance = Transportation.

Check yourself

  1. List the seven wastes using IASSC's words.
  2. A form needs five approval signatures when one person decides. Which waste?
  3. Why is overproduction called the worst waste?
  4. A mechanic walks to a distant crib for a socket set several times a day. Which waste?
  5. What is the eighth waste?
Show answers
  1. Overproduction, correction, inventory, motion, overprocessing, conveyance, waiting.
  2. Overprocessing (also creates waiting).
  3. Because it causes other wastes: inventory, conveyance, motion, waiting and often correction.
  4. Motion.
  5. Unused talent (non-utilized skills or human potential).

Key takeaways

  • IASSC seven: Overproduction, Correction, Inventory, Motion, Overprocessing, Conveyance, Waiting.
  • TIMWOOD wording: Correction = Defects, Conveyance = Transportation.
  • Overproduction is the worst; the eighth waste is unused talent.
  • Motion = people; conveyance = things. Overprocessing = more than needed; correction = fixing errors.
1.4.5:
Why this matters

5S is usually the first Lean tool an organization uses, because it is simple, visible and fast. A clean, organized workplace makes problems visible, cuts searching, improves safety and builds the discipline that every other improvement needs.

The big idea

5S is a five-step method for organizing a workplace so that everything needed is at hand, everything unneeded is gone, and anyone can tell at a glance if something is wrong. It applies to a dock, a shop, a truck cab, an office or a shared computer drive.

The five steps

1. Sort (seiri): remove what is not needed.
Go through everything in the area. Keep only what is needed for the work. Questionable items get a red tag and go to a red-tag holding area for a set time; if no one claims them, they are disposed of or moved elsewhere.

2. Straighten, or set in order (seiton): a place for everything, and everything in its place.
Arrange what remains so it is easy to find, use and return. Frequently used items closest. Use shadow boards (tool outlines painted on a board, so a missing tool is obvious), labels, floor markings, color codes. The goal: anyone can find anything in seconds.

3. Shine (seiso): clean and inspect.
Clean the area and equipment, and use cleaning as inspection: while cleaning a forklift you notice a leaking hose. Find and remove sources of dirt.

4. Standardize (seiketsu): make the first three routine.
Write down the standards: who cleans what, how often, what "good" looks like. Visual standards, such as photos of the correct layout, checklists and color codes, make deviations obvious.

5. Sustain, or self-discipline (shitsuke): make it a habit.
Training, regular 5S audits, management attention and recognition. Without sustain, the area drifts back within weeks. This is the hardest S.

The sixth S: Safety

Many organizations add Safety as a sixth S (making it "6S"), explicitly checking for hazards during each step. IASSC lists five; know Safety as the common extension.

Visual management

5S is the foundation of visual management: designing the workplace so that its status can be understood at a glance. Examples: floor lines showing where pallets go, labels on every shelf, shadow boards, color-coded bins, boards showing today's targets and actual performance, andon lights. If you need to ask or search to know whether things are normal, the workplace is not visual.

Worked example

A maintenance shop applies 5S. Match each action to its S:

ActionS
Red-tagging three broken jacks and an unused parts washerSort
Painting tool outlines on a shadow board above each benchStraighten
Daily 10-minute wipe-down of lifts, checking for leaksShine
Posting a photo of the correct bench layout with a cleaning scheduleStandardize
Monthly 5S audit scored by the supervisor, results postedSustain
Marking forklift aisles in yellow and pedestrian walkways in greenStraighten (also Safety)

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Shadow board = Straighten. Not Standardize.
  • Red tag = Sort.
  • Cleaning is also inspection (Shine).
  • Standardize = rules and visual standards; Sustain = habit, audits, discipline. Questions often confuse these two.
  • 5S is not a one-time cleanup. Without Standardize and Sustain it decays.

Check yourself

  1. List the five S's in order.
  2. Which S uses red tags?
  3. A team photographs the organized workstation and posts it as the reference. Which S?
  4. Why is cleaning called a form of inspection?
  5. Which S is usually hardest, and why?
Show answers
  1. Sort, Straighten, Shine, Standardize, Sustain (Self-discipline).
  2. Sort.
  3. Standardize.
  4. Because while cleaning you look closely at equipment and find leaks, wear and damage early.
  5. Sustain, because it depends on long-term habits and management attention rather than a one-time effort.

Key takeaways

  • Sort (red tag), Straighten (shadow boards, labels), Shine (clean and inspect), Standardize (rules and visual standards), Sustain (habit and audits).
  • Safety is a common sixth S.
  • 5S is the foundation of visual management: status visible at a glance.
